question: How much of the gap between the past-weather models and the perfect-forecast models is rain that had already fallen but was stamped with the next day?

stamps.how_to_read: correlation of daily values, 1980-2014 (IMERG: from its first day); day_before = the second series one day earlier

gain_over_control_against_stamp_offset.how_to_read: rank correlation over the basins between the stamp offset (stamps.per_basin.<gauge>.daymet_as_mix_of_nldas_days.day_before) and the NSE gain of the test over its control (models.<set>.test.basins.<gauge>.l1.nse)

rank correlation over the basins between the stamp offset (stamps.per_basin.<gauge>.daymet_as_mix_of_nldas_days.day_before) and the NSE gain of the test over its control (models.<set>.test.basins.<gauge>.l1.nse)

notes: Day stamp of Daymet - an inference from correlations of daily rain (stamps; medians of the basins), not a documented fact checked here: the Daymet rain stamped day d correlates 0.73 with NLDAS rain of the same day, 0.53 with NLDAS of the day before and 0.10 with the day after (IMERG: 0.59 / 0.55 / 0.05). A Daymet day shares its rain with two days of the other products, d-1 and d: it ends earlier than theirs, as a table built from rain gauges that are read in the morning would. The offset is not the same in every basin (stamps.per_basin): it is smallest in Myakka, FL (same day 0.78, day before 0.46, day after 0.34).

The rivers fit that reading but cannot prove it: the rise of the flow from day d-1 to day d correlates 0.58 with the Daymet rain stamped d, 0.19 with the rain stamped d-1 and 0.13 with the rain stamped d+1 (NLDAS rain: 0.42 / 0.35 / 0.03). River correlations also depend on the time the water needs to reach the gauge, so alone they could not fix a day stamp; the rain-to-rain correlations do not involve the river.

Is the NLDAS rain of the issue day known when the forecast is issued? IMERG is served by UTC day (19:00 to 19:00 local standard time in these basins; 18:00 to 18:00 in Leaf River, MS), as NASA POWER states (results/satellite_data.json). The CAMELS files do not say how hourly NLDAS rain was summed to days, so it is measured here: NLDAS rain of day d correlates 0.80 with IMERG of the same UTC day, 0.24 with the UTC day before and 0.11 with the UTC day after (day before above day after in 12 of 12 basins). The NLDAS day is therefore the UTC day or ends a little earlier - not later. The forecast is issued at the end of the local day (the day of the daily river flow), so the NLDAS value of the issue day is complete five hours or more before: its day stamp leaks nothing. This check covers 1998-2014 (IMERG has no earlier days), which holds the validation and the test years but few training years.

NLDAS itself is published a few days late, and it is made after the fact: its hourly rain is a daily rain-gauge analysis spread over the hours, with radar from 1996 and with coarser hourly gauge data before (NASA, NLDAS-2 forcing documentation). Before 1996 its day boundary may therefore be less sharp; that can change what a model learns in the training years, not how it is scored in the test years. Real-time equivalents exist (radar and gauge analyses, satellite near-real-time runs). The point here is the time stamp of the rain, not the product: the test shows the best case for rain observed up to the evening.

What the gap can hold: the 'perfect weather forecast' variants read the Daymet weather stamped t+1, t+2 and t+3 at every lead. If a Daymet day ends in the morning, most of the rain stamped t+1 had already fallen when the forecast was issued; the rest of it, and the rain stamped t+2 and t+3, fell afterwards. So the gap between the past-weather models and the perfect-forecast models 1 day ahead holds both rain that had fallen but was not yet in the table (a time-stamp gap) and rain still to come (a forecast gap). The test measures the first part.

Control: the same NLDAS rain made one day older (on issue day t the model reads the NLDAS rain of day t-1). The Daymet rain of day t correlates 0.53 with that NLDAS day and 0.73 with the next one, so the Daymet table reaches later than the control's rain: the control adds a second rain product but no later rain. Test minus control is the worth of the NLDAS rain of the issue day. That is mostly rain the Daymet table does not hold yet, but also a second estimate of the rain of the night before, which the Daymet value of day t already covers; the experiment cannot separate the two. The control alone measures what a second rain product for the days up to t-1 is worth.

Result 1 day ahead with the river gauge (test years; forecasts averaged over the seeds, lowest to highest single seed in brackets - the averaged forecast can score above every single seed). Onsets warned: 18.7% (18.0% to 18.5%) without the extra rain, 19.1% (17.7% to 20.1%) with the control, 30.0% (29.0% to 31.6%) with the NLDAS rain of the issue day, 64.3% with the perfect forecast: the rain of the issue day closes 25% of that gap, 24% beyond the control; every single seed with it is above every seed without it and every seed of the control. False warnings among the onset warnings, in the same order: 59%, 64%, 63%, 26%. Median NSE: 0.590 (0.542 to 0.598), 0.605 (0.575 to 0.596), 0.674 (0.617 to 0.665), 0.865: 31% of the gap, 25% beyond the control; every single seed with it is above every seed without it and every seed of the control. Basin by basin the NSE is higher than without the extra rain in 5 of 12 basins and higher than with the control in 6 (median basin difference -0.006 and +0.000): the difference of two medians and the median of the basin differences need not agree. The perfect-forecast model is an upper bound in what it knows, not in every basin's score: it scores below the model without the extra rain in 1 of 12 basins (not examined here). 2 and 3 days ahead: 4% and 1% of the NSE gap and 6% and 4% of the onset-warning gap.

Result 1 day ahead without the river gauge (test years; forecasts averaged over the seeds, lowest to highest single seed in brackets - the averaged forecast can score above every single seed). Onsets warned: 17.2% (16.2% to 19.5%) without the extra rain, 19.5% (17.5% to 19.6%) with the control, 31.6% (30.8% to 33.2%) with the NLDAS rain of the issue day, 69.9% with the perfect forecast: the rain of the issue day closes 27% of that gap, 23% beyond the control; every single seed with it is above every seed without it and every seed of the control. False warnings among the onset warnings, in the same order: 83%, 79%, 72%, 50%. Median NSE: 0.443 (0.355 to 0.434), 0.497 (0.448 to 0.490), 0.516 (0.417 to 0.524), 0.722: 26% of the gap, 7% beyond the control; the single seeds overlap those of the model without it or of the control. Basin by basin the NSE is higher than without the extra rain in 10 of 12 basins and higher than with the control in 9 (median basin difference +0.072 and +0.066): the difference of two medians and the median of the basin differences need not agree. The perfect-forecast model is an upper bound in what it knows, not in every basin's score: it scores below the model without the extra rain in 2 of 12 basins (not examined here). 2 and 3 days ahead: 8% and 1% of the NSE gap and 6% and 4% of the onset-warning gap.

How far the test reaches: the share closed 1 day ahead is not the whole time-stamp part of the gap. The NLDAS day ends at 19:00 local time or a little earlier, so rain of the last five hours or more of the issue day is in neither model, and what is left of the gap is therefore not all rain still to come. NLDAS and Daymet are also different products, so the split is approximate.

Does the gain follow the day stamp? 1 day ahead, the NSE gain of the test over its control is compared, basin by basin, with the offset of the Daymet day (the share of the NLDAS day before in daymet_as_mix_of_nldas_days): rank correlation +0.90 with the river gauge, +0.66 without it. 12 basins that share storms: a description, not a proof.

Same settings and seeds as 04_lstm_all.py (results/lstm_all.json, key config): the trainings differ from its models only in the extra input column. The comparison sets lstm_w, lstm_wq, lstm_wf, lstm_wqf are read from its prediction files, not retrained. All sets are compared on identical days (coverage 1.0, asserted).

Fair test: nothing is chosen here. The settings were chosen by 04_lstm_all.py on the validation years, the trainer picks each stopping point on the validation years, and the test years are only scored. The closure table is test years only; models.<set>.val holds the validation-year scores of the four new sets.

runtime_s is the time of the training run from start to end. That run did not record how long it waited for the CPU behind another job, so runtime_s includes the wait; training_seconds is the time of the trainings alone.

This file was written by --rescore: every score, table and note and the figure were recomputed from the saved prediction sets lstm_<set>_s<seed> without training again; the training records in per_seed, n_trainings, training_seconds and runtime_s are those of the training run. rescore_runtime_s is the time of this pass.
